in_text_mentions: PLE is the commonest photosensitive disorder, characterized by an intermittent eruption of non-scarring pruritic erythematous papules, vesicles or plaques (Figure 1) that develop within hours of ultraviolet radiation (UVR) exposure of patient skin. The disease is dependent on genetic susceptibility, as well as environmental component, such as type of exposure. PLE appears to cluster in families: it has been estimated that the prevalence of PLE was 21 and 18% in monozygotic and dizygotic twins, respectively (1). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E histology from elbow eruption in article confirming spring elbow rash as PLE variant; panel A shows spared epidermis with superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate matching vocabulary. B: H&E histology from same PLE-variant elbow case; panel B shows superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. C: High-power H&E of dermo-epidermal junction in PLE-variant elbow case showing lymphocytic infiltrate, consistent with perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate. D: High-power H&E showing lymphocytic infiltrate clustered around vessels in PLE-variant elbow case, matching perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.

in_text_mentions: In all cases, histological examinations revealed perivascular superficial and deep lymphocytic infiltrates in the dermis, along with variable degrees of dermal edema. Epidermal changes were present in four of the patients, along with mild spongiosis and parakeratosis (Figure 4). The anti-CD123 marker staining was negative for all patients (images not shown).

symmetrical, maculopapular, and pruritic skin eruption on the elbows

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Panel A shows elbow rash in series confirming spring/summer elbow rash as variant of polymorphous light eruption by photoprovocation and histopathology; maculopapular eruption with erythematous plaque and papules. B: Self-taken photo of elbow spring rash in PLE-variant cohort; shows erythema with papules consistent with described maculopapular eruption. C: Self-taken photo of elbow spring rash in PLE-variant series; shows papular eruption on elbow. D: Clinical image of elbow spring rash during first interview in PLE-variant cohort; shows papular lesions. E: Self-taken photo of elbow spring rash in PLE-variant series; shows papular eruption on elbow.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical images of spring rash on the elbows in five patients who underwent photobiological studies. Some of the patients' photos (B, C, E) were self-taken before their visit to the hospital. They were asymptomatic during their first visit prior to undergoing photobiological studies. Patients (A, D) presented with some lesions during the first interview, as shown in the images.
in_text_mentions: with phototype III, and one patient with phototype IV. All patients reported a symmetrical, maculopapular, and pruritic skin eruption on the elbows that began in spring within hours/days of sun exposure and disappeared after several days without sun exposure, and topical treatment with corticosteroids was administered in some cases (Table 1; Figure 1). Subsequently, they presented similar recurrent outbreaks that were always related to sun exposure. All the patients studied had previously undergone blood tests, including porphyrins, IgE, and antinuclear antibodies, and the results were normal.
